stances.claim: Reverting to manual elections to escape automation glitches would be a far worse outcome than the glitches themselves, because manual voting was structurally vulnerable to a long catalogue of cheating modalities -- illegible ballots, identifying marks, lansadera, dagdag-bawas in ERs and SOVs, ballot-box theft, preproclamation controversies -- that automation has either eliminated or rendered visible.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-history rebuttal (don't compare automation to perfection; compare it to what it replaced)

stances.claim: Namfrel's hybrid proposal (voters write on ballots, manual precinct count, electronic transmission to safely located servers) gains precinct-level transparency at the cost of reintroducing the entire manual-era attack surface; if the goal is transparency, the answer is a less-opaque automation, not a return to manual voting.

With three years until the next elections, Comelec has the runway to minimize glitches and reduce the opacity of the Smartmatic system -- addressing Namfrel's valid transparency concerns without 'risking the horrors of manual voting.'

Imperfection is the universal condition of complex computer systems -- banking, airlines, logistics -- and the responsible engineering posture is to minimize imperfection iteratively, not to demolish the system.

notable_anecdotes: The taxonomy of 'identifying marks' that allowed manual-era cheaters to verify the bribed/coerced voter actually voted correctly -- peculiar name sequencing across multiple races, inclusion of middle initials or full names of favored candidates -- physicalizing how voter intimidation was made auditable to the perpetrator.

The 'lansadera' technique in full mechanical detail -- a genuine ballot smuggled out of the precinct (often with the Board of Election Inspectors' connivance), filled up in a safe house, given to a voter who casts it and brings back the blank he was issued, repeated 'on and on' -- captures the systemic complicity that automation broke.

The 'wholesale' SOV manipulation arithmetic -- '1,000 to 10,000, or vice versa, spelled victory or defeat at the district or provincial level' -- making concrete how a single digit change at the canvassing level translated into political outcomes.

one_paragraph_summary: Responding to the post-2019-polls clamor -- from election watchdogs, losing candidates, and millennial voters -- to revert to manual elections, Panganiban catalogues why the 'mano-mano' era was structurally worse than the glitchy present. Under manual voting, ballots depended on voter penmanship and were frequently invalidated for illegibility; the 'guns, goons and gold' could verify coerced votes through identifying marks, peculiar name sequencing, and middle-initial inclusions; the 'lansadera' scheme cycled genuine ballots through safe houses with Board of Election Inspectors complicity; manual counting lasted into the wee hours with ballots misread or untallied, and ballot boxes were stolen or doused with acid; and 'wholesale' cheating altered Election Returns and Statements of Votes -- the classic dagdag-bawas -- with one-digit changes flipping town, district, or provincial outcomes through tedious preproclamation controversies that automation has eliminated. Even Namfrel's proposed hybrid system -- manual writing, manual precinct count, electronic transmission for consolidation -- would gain precinct-level transparency at the cost of reintroducing the entire manual-era vulnerability surface; if transparency is the goal, the answer is a less-opaque automation, not a manual return. With three years before the next elections, Comelec has the runway to reduce glitches and answer 'Namfrel's valid concerns without risking the horrors of manual voting.' No computer system in banking, airlines, or logistics is perfect; the engineering posture is to minimize imperfection, not to demolish the system.
